summary:
Denmark permits legal gender recognition by self-declaration, with no medical evaluation required, a regime in force since 2014 and the first of its kind in Europe. Non-binary people may obtain an 'X' marker in passports, and trans people determine their own legal gender markers.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited. The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services; workplace protection on the basis of gender identity has been in place since 2015, and fair-housing protection on that ground has held throughout the monitored period.

Same-sex couples may marry and adopt. Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships, in 1989, and marriage equality followed in 2012.

On 10 September 2024 the Danish Supreme Court held that serving a sentence in a men's prison department does not violate the human rights of a trans inmate. That judgment is the leading Danish authority on where trans detainees are placed, and it is the single most consequential ruling for a visitor who is remanded or convicted.

The Danish Institute for Human Rights reports that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time a report is made, which bears directly on a visitor who is targeted. Its LGBT+ barometer records that 38% of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech directed at sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics recurs every year.

Violence against trans people is documented. In July 2024 a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen. The UN Committee Against Torture, in its eighth periodic review, found that some trans people, QTIBIPOC and migrants report denial of access to spaces and services as well as threats.

Denmark's record on arrest and asylum is favourable on the available indicators: freedoms against arbitrary arrest based on gender identity were affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024, and in February 2013 a Guatemalan trans woman became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark, refused return over her gender identity after citing police attacks and threats tied to her trans activism.
tangentialFactors:
Anti-trans discourse intensified in Denmark while parliament debated lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition, according to the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024. The same review notes that the UN Committee Against Torture urged the authorities to provide psychosocial counselling and to remedy intersex interventions.

Denmark is routinely ranked among the world's strongest jurisdictions for LGBTQ+ rights, and activists credit the self-ID law with cooling the trans debate rather than provoking a rollback. In March 2025 the country signed a UN resolution against discrimination on grounds of sex characteristics.

In August 2024 the government announced a plan to strengthen recognition of multi-parent families of three or four parents, an area of family law adjacent to but distinct from trans status.
localsOnly:
40% of LGBTI students aged 15 to 25 reported self-harm in the past year, a rate two to three times that of their classmates, per the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025. This is a resident and youth-welfare indicator rather than a visitor-facing one.

Workplace anti-discrimination law has covered gender identity since 2015 and fair-housing protection has been in place across the monitored period, which matters for residents and long-stay residents rather than short-term visitors.

The multi-parent family reform announced in August 2024 and the psychosocial counselling and intersex remedy measures urged by the UN Committee Against Torture are domestic policy questions affecting residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Conversion-therapy status is unresolved in the sources. One source records a ban in force since 2023, while another states there is no ban and that a bill was revived in August 2026. The current legal position should be verified against the Danish statute before publication.

Whether Danish police have since been required to flag hate-crime motivation at the point of reporting is not sourced; the inventory only establishes the Danish Institute for Human Rights finding that no such obligation existed.

The scope of the Supreme Court's 10 September 2024 prison-placement ruling — whether it extends to pre-operative, non-binary or intersex detainees, and to remand rather than convicted prisoners — is not addressed in the available material.

The sources do not state whether Denmark's asylum practice toward trans claimants after the 2013 Fernanda Milan decision has been consistent; only that single early case is documented here.
